sections.h2: How a Columbia, TN owner can turn a house into cash fast
sections.html:
Your options: a direct cash offer, an agent, or a do-it-yourself sale. Cash is quickest, since no underwriter signs off and the buyer accepts the property in its present shape.

Columbia is Maury County's seat, on the Duck River south of Nashville. The 2020 census counted 41,690 people in April, a 2024 special census found 48,885, and the mid-2025 estimate is 50,072. New residents keep coming, but a house with leaky roofing or an outdated kitchen can still sit unsold.

  • Cash buyer: the shortest path, with repair cost already folded into the offer.
  • Agent listing: the widest exposure, along with inspections and lender deadlines.
  • Self-sale: the commission is yours, and so is every document.

Whichever route appeals, ask first for a mortgage payoff letter and a tax balance.

Owner occupancy in Columbia is 63.3%, and 87.8% of residents age one or older stayed put for the past year. Median rent is $1,197 monthly, and a midpoint owned home is worth $308,700.

With a 28 minute average trip to work, buyers will ask how far your street is from the main roads.

Households average 2.46 people and 25.6% of residents are children, so expect questions on bedrooms, yard size and school zone. The public schools come under Maury County Public Schools. Owners of older houses should also ask the city planning office about historic-district rules for their address before telling buyers what they can change outside.

  • Have the bedroom and bathroom count, lot size and year built on one page.
  • Note which internet providers reach the house.
  • Look up the school zone with Maury County Public Schools.

Columbia's houses range from antebellum homes to postwar neighborhoods. If you know when yours was built, say so, and keep any record of roof, wiring or plumbing updates handy.

Columbia grew up beside the Duck River, the longest river lying wholly inside Tennessee, so a lot near the water needs a flood-zone check before you price it.

  • Look over the yard after a downpour and note where water pools.
  • Ask your insurance agent for the flood-zone status.
  • Keep receipts for furnace and air conditioner service.

sections.h2: How the Maury County tax bill works
sections.html:
Each October the Maury County Trustee mails bills to whoever held the property on January 1. Payment opens the first Monday of October and runs to the end of February. A 1.5% charge begins March 1 and rises monthly, and anything unpaid by April 1 lands in Chancery Court.

At One Public Square (931-375-2201), the trustee accepts partial payments and can set up monthly bank debits. Paying online adds a 2.5% fee that goes to the vendor. Interest still applies when a bill goes astray, since notices are not required by state law.

When a sale happens partway through the year, your closing company splits the bill. Get the exact balance from the trustee before you sign.

Property in Maury County is revalued on a four-year cycle; the current reappraisal year is 2026. The Assessor's office, 6 Public Square (931-375-4001), keeps the January 1 value from the last reappraisal and layers on later improvements.

To estimate a bill, take the appraised value, apply the class assessment ratio, then apply the rate the Maury County Commission sets. A value that looks wrong can be appealed first to the county's local board and then to the state-level board.

A seller in the next year or two should tell the buyer about the new value, since the next bill may not match the last one.

sections.h2: Where the deed is filed after a Columbia sale
sections.html:
Filing happens at the Maury County Register of Deeds, a constitutional office responsible for permanent archiving and public access to records. The county website has a fee calculator.

Recording triggers state tax in two forms, a realty transfer tax and a mortgage tax, both collected by the register.

Inherited the house? Give the closing company the probate papers so it can see who may sign. Check the exact filing fee with the register before closing.

sections.h2: Cash offer or listing in Columbia?
sections.html:
Cash works well for a worn roof, an old kitchen, a tenant in place, or any case where speed beats top price. Listing works for a sound house and an owner who can sit through showings and a buyer's loan process. Put the two side by side by asking what you would actually keep: the sale price minus repairs, holding costs, commission and the taxes still owed.

A month of carrying an empty house adds up through utilities, insurance and yard care, and the tax bill keeps running. Get each buyer's price and closing date in writing, and find out from the closing company how long title work will run. If the house was inherited, hand over the probate papers at the start so nobody is surprised by a missing signature near the end.

Sequence matters. You request a payoff letter from your lender and a tax balance from the Maury County Trustee, then assemble the deed, your newest tax bill and a list of owners. When an offer is accepted, the closing company checks who may sign, apportions the year's tax and carries the deed to the Register of Deeds. With cash there is no loan approval and no post-inspection repair list, so title work is the main thing that sets the date.

On signing day take a photo ID, your keys and any garage openers. When the recorded deed comes back, ask the closing company for a copy and file it with your tax papers.

sections.h2: Selling with taxes owed in Maury County
sections.html:
Back taxes will not block a Columbia sale. Closing takes the balance out of your proceeds, so nobody asks for a separate check. Call the trustee for the exact figure, including the monthly interest that begins March 1, and ask whether the account was sent to Chancery Court after April 1.

Short on cash before you sell? The trustee takes partial payments and can set up monthly bank debits. Paying online adds a vendor fee of 2.5%, so paying in person at One Public Square avoids it, and it is worth doing before the March 1 interest date. Keep every receipt and hand copies to the closing company so it can see what is already settled.

faqs.q: Can I sell a Columbia house that needs repairs?
faqs.a: Yes. A direct buyer takes it as is and lowers the offer by the repair cost, which spares you contractors and open houses. Compare that number with what a repaired listing would net.

faqs.q: When does a Maury County tax bill go delinquent?
faqs.a: On March 1. Interest starts at 1.5% and rises monthly, and unpaid accounts are sent to Chancery Court on April 1.

faqs.q: Is Maury County being reappraised now?
faqs.a: Yes, 2026 is the current reappraisal year, and values update every four years. Disagreements go first to the local board of equalization.

faqs.q: Can I pay my Maury County tax in installments?
faqs.a: In a way. The trustee takes partial payments and monthly bank debits, though any balance left after February picks up interest on March 1.

faqs.q: Where do I get a copy of my Columbia deed?
faqs.a: Ask the Maury County Register of Deeds, which keeps recorded deeds permanently. A copy may also be in your closing papers.
